Crypt of the NecroDancer is a very innovative game that somehow manages put together Roguelike dungeon games and rhythm games into one well polished and fun game.

So far in my playtime I have found no bugs or issues or really even anything that felt unfair. The rules of the game make sense, are fair, are fun, and still manage to be challenging.

The inclusion of being able to add any song you want to the game really brings this game over the top. On top of that they added support for the steam workshop for mods. Allowing customizability is always something games should do.

If you are waiting for one game or another to come out, or you just want a game you can play for 5 minutes every so often to chill (No not Netflix and chill) well this game will be great for you!

-it has a great soundtrack
-Superd pixel art
-Awsome different bosses and characters to play
And find out the rest. :D

But one bad point for this game, is the hardness of the levels, which may make you rage (it did for me...)

Good luck in your quest and have fun

While offering an innovative rhythmic take on roguelikes, Crypt of the Necrodancer falls short in several key aspects. The game's difficulty curve can feel unreasonably steep, especially when transitioning between characters like Aria, whose punishing gameplay lacks the advantages of other characters. This can make progression feel more like a chore than a satisfying challenge.

Moreover, the game's presentation of information is lacking. Players are left to decipher the effects of items, shrines, and enemies through trial and error, often resulting in frustrating and unnecessary deaths. This lack of clarity can hinder the learning process and discourage further exploration.

Combat is also problematic. The need to memorize enemy attack patterns and execute precise moves can feel like homework, stifling the organic and enjoyable aspects of combat. This issue, combined with the lack of intuitive response to enemy actions, can lead to repetitive and tedious engagements, undermining the potential for engaging gameplay.

Crypt of the NecroDancer's challenging difficulty spikes, lack of clear information, and often tedious combat mechanics can overshadow its innovative concept, making it a less appealing choice for players seeking a balanced and enjoyable roguelike experience. Everything combined, I don't think I'll be coming back to play more. Give it a shot if you *really* think you will like it but my general opinion is to pass on this one.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is an amazing indie game that, even though was lauched 10 years ago (written in 2025), holds up greatly as a roguelike that bases itself in music. Even though the whole game works around this, it still blows me away that even with this higher standard how good the soundtrack is. It's a perfect game to spend like 5-10 minutes, and presents an unbelievable challenge to those who dare to master its mechanics and complete all the achievements available. 100% recommended, and awesome that Brace Yourself Games still keeps updating the game from time to time.

(I've played more than 3 hours, I just uninstalled and reinstalled because of some Steam issues.) If a game makes music integral to its experience, it can be incredibly powerful in a variety of ways. This game makes music not only integral to the experience, but also to the technical aspects of the gameplay itself. It doesn't stop at becoming emotionally invested in the music and sound design of this game; you're made a part of the music and the sound design, driven and enveloped by these things. Although the player is, as expected, pitted against all the horrors of the Crypt, they are also fundamentally bound to these enemies by the rhythms and beats that drive all movement in the game. The intimacy between the player and the enemies in the game is what makes learning their movements and defeating them so engaging: it's as if each enemy teaches you their own "dance," and you overcome challenges by adding more to your repertoire. If you aren't interested in me going "me smart, me use big word, game good," then the TLDR is this game is super fun, the music is great, and it's the first time I've enjoyed the idea of playing the same stages over and over again to improve. It's definitely worth the price - frankly, it's worth a lot more.

While Crypt of the NecroDancer certainly provides a proof of concept, a sweet soundtrack by Danny Baranowsky, and the best game based off a bad pun, the buyer should beware two things.

1. It is Early Access. The typical selling points and detractions apply here.
2. SilverString Media, a company notoriously known for its corruption, nepotism, and hypocrisy, particularily in the indie games scene, provided "story consultation." A quick five minutes of research into SilverString shows who, among their "advisors", a consumer might object to profiting off of their purchase.

These two things are a shame, since the developer themself, Ryan Clark of Brace Yourself Games, is a superbly funny, nice, and committed programmer who does his best to engage his community. If you can overcome those two points, this is a good jump into the Early Access pool.

So I kept seeing this game and wondering why people liked it. Just watching the video and looking at the pics didn't quite convey the fun of the game. I thought I'd give it a try since it was on sale for $2.99. Well f#$# me I couldn't stop playing the damn thing. Highly addictive. The rhythm thing really adds a whole new challenge to the game. It's a lot trickier than it looks. It's not just some dumb mindless moving to a beat, you really have to choose your movements very carefully and strategically, all while keeping time with the beat. I saw one negative review and the person said they are a "musician" and they knew for a fact that the rhythm was not correctly synched or something like that. Well, I'm also a musician of 27 years, have a degree in music and teach people music for a living, and I can tell you the other reviewer is wrong, there is nothing wrong with the rhythm synchronization. I just played for like 3 hours straight and only missed a couple beats because of mistakes on my part. I had no problem synchronizing to the beat for almost a continuous 20-30 mins for each run that I did. When you first play the game it goes through this synchronization process, if you do that right you should have no problems with the rhythm synch.

As a general rule, I avoid roguelites; my preference in games runs toward experiences that continually progress toward an intended end, not through evolving gameplay so much as "story" and its associations. This game is one of the few exemptions, for two reasons. First, it manages a rectification of the roguelite formula with a event themed progression. Second, and more relevantly, it comes with one of the best and most diverse soundtracks in all of gaming. Strong melodies with strong arrangement serves as the foundation for numerous remixes across several different styles, both as part of the game and beyond. But even if that wasn't enough, there's also included the ingeniously creative mechanic/musical experiment of a synthesized instrumental vocalist: the Shopkeeper. I'd argue that, for this alone, the game is worth experiencing.
This is easily one of the most enjoyable roguelikes out there. Great for anyone who considers themselves a fan of the genre, but make sure you have a good sense of rhythm!

I'll keep it brief, this game is hard. Not just keeping the rhythm, that's the easy part. The hard part is being able to play a roguelike quickly, to multi-task everything and be 10 steps ahead of every encounter. At first you will hate the game, you will swear at it, call it bullshit.

To beat the game, you have to know every in and out, both what items do and what enemies attack patterns are. Not knowing a single attack pattern can literally end your run. You also need a fair bit of luck, not to say that you need luck to beat the game, but that you probably need luck to beat the game if you're not a master. Just like games like spelunky, you need a perfect master of skill and luck.

But the game is fire if you don't get frustrated easily and are willing to sit through one of the hardest games of your life.

This is a really fun dungeon crawler. The mechanics are quite basic. Everything moves to the beat, including you. You must figure out the patterns of movement each enemy type uses, and exploit them in order to attack without being hit yourself. The controls are very simple. In fact, the entire game can be played using only the arrow keys.
Games are quick and action-packed. Very good for people who favour shorter sessions. The music is also excellent, with a surprising amount of variety. The game does support using your own MP3s to replace the game's own music, although you may have some issues if your track lacks a strong, constant beat.
Overall, I would highly recommend this.
